title: Novel Potassium Binders in Reduction of Hyperkalemia and Optimization of RAAS Inhibitors Treatment in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease or Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
abstract: BackgroundRenin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) and its combination therapy are essential supportive treatments for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure (HF). Hyperkalemia (HK) is the major safety concern associated with the treatments, which often leads to RAASi dose reduction or discontinuation, thereby compromising cardiovascular protective effects. Although novel potassium binders (NPBs) are recommended by current guidelines for the treatment of HK, systematic evidence is needed to guide their use in RAASi optimization and HK management. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the incidence of HK in patients with CKD or HF who received RAASi and the efficacy of NPBs in RAASi optimization. MethodsPubMed, Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 1, 2011 to December 31, 2023. Any studies of adult patients with CKD or HF who received RAASi were included in systematic review of HK incidence and risk factors (part 1). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of NPBs in patients with CKD or HF were included in meta-analysis on the efficacy of novel potassium binders (NPBs) (part 2). The primary outcome was optimization of RAASi therapy with NPBs. A pooled analysis was conducted in part 1. Network meta-analyses using a random-effects model were performed in part 2.ResultsA total of 83 studies (24 with CKD, 54 with HF, and 5 with CKD and HF) were included in part 1 and 8 RCTs (2 with CKD, 4 with HF, and 2 with CKD and HF) were included in part 2. The pooled HK incidence was 10.7% overall at any criteria and in all patients who received RAASi. The highest incidence of HK was observed with the combination of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi)/angiotensin ii receptor blockers (ARBs)/angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNi)+ mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) (24.4%), followed by the triple therapy ACEi/ARB/ARNi+ sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i)+MRA (10.9%), and ACEi/ARB/ARNi + SGLT2i (2.2%). Novel potassium binders improved RAASi optimization by 38% compared with placebo (risk ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.16–1.65). Additionally, NPBs decreased the incidence of HK by 28% and reduced the level of potassium by 0.71 mEq/L. The CKD population showed a higher optimization rate than the HF population (84% vs 29%).ConclusionThe RAASi treatment was associated with high prevalence of HK, especially in bigeminal and triple therapy. The NPBs were effective in RAASi optimization and HK management, especially among the CKD population.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40265-025-02198-6.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Hyperkalemia (HK) is a common and potentially life-threatening condition characterized by elevated serum potassium levels. It is frequently observed in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or heart failure (HF) []. Renin-angiotensin aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASis) are a class of drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system, which include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs). Renin-angiotensin aldosterone system inhibitors, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are commonly used medications for the treatment of CKD and HF due to their ability to mitigate disease progression, reduce morbidity, and improve survival outcomes []. However, RAASi and ARNI affect the production or activity of aldosterone, reduce aldosterone secretion, thereby limiting urinary excretion of potassium and predisposing to HK []. Their use is often limited or discontinued due to HK risk, which is the most common electrolyte disorder in patients with CKD or HF [, ].

The dilemma of balancing RAASi therapy and managing HK has underscored the need for effective therapeutic strategies to maintain optimal treatment. Potassium binders, such as patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC), are used to manage chronic HK with minimal side effects, thereby facilitating the optimization of disease management with a very low occurrence of side effects []. Although current guidelines recommend potassium binders as a treatment for HK, several clinical questions still persist with regard to their use in RAASi optimization, such as appropriate initiation thresholds (serum K+ levels), dose titration strategy during RAASi up-titration, and long-term safety beyond 12 months of treatment.

The present systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the incidence of HK during RAASi treatment and examined the efficacy of novel potassium binders (NPBs) on the optimization of RAASi therapy, as well as their impact on potassium levels and HK event reduction in patients with CKD or HF.

sections.title: Methods
sections.text:
We conducted a systemic review and meta-analysis to examine two aspects: (i) the incidence of HK in patients with CKD or HF receiving RAASi (part 1), and (ii) the efficacy of NPB in RAASi optimization (part 2). For part 1, we performed a pooled analysis, while for part 2, we conducted meta-analyses using a random-effects model. The meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024594521).

First, we searched PubMed, Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for studies published between January 1, 2011, to December 31, 2023. In addition, we conducted manual searching for prespecified conference proceedings, including American Society of Nephrology Congress (ASN) Kidney Week 2024, 61st European Renal Association (ERA) congress 2024, European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress 2024, American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2024. Part 1 included studies that involved adult patients with CKD or HF who received RAASi, while part 2 focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of potassium binders in patients with CKD or HF. Detailed search strategies are provided in Online Resource 1 (see electronic supplementary material [ESM]).

After an initial literature search, we removed duplicates, screened titles and abstracts to eliminate irrelevant articles. The remaining articles were subjected to a full-text review and studies were removed based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Two independent reviewers conducted this process, with a third reviewer resolving any discrepancies.

Studies satisfying the following criteria were included: articles published in the English language that report at least one predefined result of interest, human studies, interventional studies and observational studies in any clinical setting (e.g., inpatients at discharge, outpatients, primary care, hospital), and RCTs for comparing different treatments to manage HK. Studies were excluded if they were not written in the English language, animal studies, in vitro studies, or included patients who did not have CKD or HF.

The primary outcome was the optimization of RAASi therapy with potassium binders. Secondary outcomes included HK incidence in patients receiving RAASi, RAASi dose adjustment after HK, and comparisons between different HK treatments (e.g., HK incidence, adverse events [AEs], reduction in serum potassium levels, incidence of hypokalemia, diarrhea, constipation, nausea or vomiting, hypomagnesemia, edema, serious AEs, and AEs leading to discontinuation).

All data were extracted by one statistician and independently verified by another. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus, with a third reviewer available to arbitrate if necessary. Data extraction was conducted using standardized data extraction forms. Extracted information included first author name, PubMed identification number, clinical trial registration number, year of journal article publication, study treatments, duration of follow-up, sample size, baseline characteristics (age, gender distribution), clinical characteristics, and efficacy outcomes. The Cochrane risk of bias tool was used to assess the risk of bias of this network meta-analysis.

Both qualitative and quantitative data included in the standardized data extraction forms were transferred to the predefined Excel tables. The extraction tables are designed to capture the study characteristics (authors’ names, year of publication, study type, inclusion criteria, and study population), participant characteristics (sample size, patient demographics [i.e., age and sex], and clinical characteristics), intervention details (type of therapy, treatment regimen details, and follow-up and treatment duration), relevant outcomes (proportion of patients who received RAASi after follow-up, different treatments to correct HK, comparison of different potassium binding agents, AEs, all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events) and any other relevant data.

Descriptive statistics were used to describe the incidence and risk factors of HK. As these variables are intended as a scoping review, no synthesis of the evidence or evaluation of the quality of the studies will be carried out.

The meta-analysis was conducted to assess the efficacy of NPBs on the optimization of RAASi therapy, using R Studio software, version 4.3.3. For continuous variables, mean differences (MD) and standard deviations (SD) were calculated. For dichotomous variables, effect sizes were estimated using the risk ratio (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity among studies in the model was analyzed, with I2 values indicating different levels of heterogeneity: mild (I2 < 25%), moderate (25 ≤ I2 < 50%), and severe (I2 ≥ 50%). Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s tests and by inspecting the symmetry of funnel plots. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. We performed sensitivity analyses on efficacy outcomes with (1) a leave-one-out approach to ensure that results were not dependent on a single study, and (2) subgroup analysis according to the population (i.e., HF, CKD, HF and CKD) and the type of NPBs (i.e., patiromer, SZC).

sections.title: Results
sections.text:
A total of 119 studies with 449,214 patients (199,770 with CKD, 238,053 with HF, and 11,391 with CKD and HF) were included in this part [, –]. Based on 83 studies (24 for CKD, 54 for HF, and 5 for CKD and HF) with different HK thresholds (potassium level ≥ 5.0 mmol/L, ≥ 5.5 mmol/L, or ≥ 6.0 mmol/L, respectively), the pooled HK incidence was 10.0% in all patients who received RAASi, with 12.0% in patients with CKD, 9.2% in patients with HF, and 10.9% in patients with CKD and HF (Table 1). The incidence of HK was 12.9%, 13.7%, and 5.1% at a cut-off of potassium level of 5.0 mmol/L, 5.5 mmol/L and 6.0 mmol/L, respectively. Different combination therapies also affected HK incidence, with the highest rate (24.4%) observed in the ACEi/ARB/ARNi + MRA group at a potassium level of ≥ 5.0 mmol/L, followed by the triple therapy ACEi/ARB/ARNi + SGLT2i + MRA (10.9%), while the ACEi/ARB/ARNi + SGLT2i combination showed the lowest HK incidence (2.2%) (Table 1). The proportion of HF patients who discontinued RAASi treatment varied from 16.7 to 100%, and the percentage among CKD patients was 0–66.8% (Online Resource 2, see ESM). Notably, 16.7–61.1% of patients were reported to have discontinued MRA and 2.7–62.6% of patients discontinued ACEi/ARB + MRA.

Three studies reported outcomes related to RAASi adjustment after occurrence of HK. They revealed that the discontinuation of MRA due to HK was associated with a lower risk of recurrent HK but resulted in a higher risk of AEs and all-cause mortality in HF patients [, ]. In addition, RAASi discontinuation was linked to a higher risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular (CV) mortality in CKD patients [].

An overview of the 22 studies [, , , –, –] that estimated risk factors of HK is presented in Online Resource 3 (see ESM). A high risk of HK in HF or CKD patients was significantly associated with RAASi use, age, diabetes, elevated baseline potassium levels, and other factors. In general, higher risk estimates were observed more frequently in observational studies than in interventional trials.

The PRISMA checklist and flow diagrams are shown in Online Resource 4 (see ESM) and Fig. 1. Eight RCTs were included, and a total of 2564 patients were randomly allocated to receive NPB or placebo [–]. Study characteristics are shown in Online Resource 5 (see ESM). The included RCTs were assessed for risk of bias through the RoB2 tool, as per Cochrane’s recommendations (Online Resource 6, see ESM). Only OPAL HK and CRYSTAL trials were considered at risk of some bias, while other trials were at low risk.Fig. 1Flow diagram. NMA network meta-analysis

Seven studies were included in the analysis of optimization of RAASi therapy in HF/CKD patients. The use of NPBs was associated with a 38% improvement in RAASi therapy optimization compared with placebo (RR: 1.38, 95% CI 1.16–1.65; p = 0.0002; I2 = 80.2%; Fig. 2A), indicating that a larger proportion of patients receiving NPB remained on RAASi therapy at the conclusion of the studies compared to those receiving placebo.Fig. 2Forest plots for optimization of RAASi therapy. The analysis of HK events included five studies and showed that NPB significantly reduced the risk of HK events by 28% compared to placebo (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.58–0.89; p = 0.0020; I2 = 21.4%; Fig. 2B). Additionally, NPB resulted in a greater reduction in mean potassium levels compared to placebo with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of − 0.71 mEq/L (95% CI − 1.13 to − 0.30; p = 0.0007; I2 = 83.2%; Fig. 2C).

There was no difference between NPB and placebo groups in the risk of any AEs (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.93–1.06; p = 0.9101; I2 = 2.9%; Fig. 3A), AEs leading to discontinuation (RR 1.20; 95% CI 0.78–1.83; p = 0.4097; I2 = 0%; Online Resource 7, see ESM), or serious AEs (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.77–1.29; p = 0.9802; I2 = 0%; Online Resource 7, see ESM).Fig. 3Forest plots for any AEs and hypokalemia events. Regarding specific AEs, no significant differences were observed between NPB and placebo in the risk of diarrhea (RR 1.32; 95% CI 0.78–2.23; p = 0.2941; I2 = 0%; Online Resource 7, see ESM), nausea or vomiting (RR 1.66; 95% CI 0.56–4.92; p = 0.3619; I2 = 0%; Online Resource 7, see ESM), or hypomagnesemia (RR 1.67; 95% CI 0.42–6.63; p = 0.4632; I2 = 56.4%; Online Resource 7, see ESM). However, NPBs were associated with an increased incidence of hypokalemia (RR 4.96; 95% CI 1.65–14.88; p = 0.0043; I2 = 0%; Fig. 3B), edema (RR 3.10;95% CI 1.05–9.22; p = 0413; I2 = 0%; Online Resource 7, see ESM), and constipation (RR 2.26; 95% CI 1.01–5.05; p = 0.0470; I2 = 0%; Online Resource 7, see ESM).

Subgroup analyses were conducted based on patient population and type of NPB used. Patients with CKD (RR = 1.84; 95% CI 1.14–2.97) showed a higher RAASi optimization rate than the HF population (RR = 1.29; 95% CI 0.99–1.67) (Fig. 4A). Meanwhile, HF patients had a higher risk of hypokalemia events (RR = 8.65; 95% CI 2.05, 36.53) than CKD patients (RR = 1.07; 95% CI 0.07–16.32) (Fig. 4B). Compared with patiromer (RR = 1.25; 95% CI 1.09–1.43), SZC was associated with a higher RAASi optimization rate (RR = 1.60; 95% CI 1.07–2.40) (Fig. 5A). Publication bias for all outcomes was assessed (Online Resource 10 and 11, see ESM). Egger’s test revealed potential publication bias for the optimization of RAASi therapy, nausea/vomiting, and potassium level reduction. However, no significant risk of publication bias was detected for the other outcomes. It is important to note that due to the low number of studies included in the present meta-analysis, we could not entirely rule out publication bias, as suggested by the Egger’s test values. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we conducted sensitivity analyses on all outcomes, which demonstrated consistent effects regardless of the exclusion of any single study, as shown in Online Resource 12 (see ESM).

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text:
The systematic review and meta-analyses offer valuable insights into the incidence of HK among patients with CKD or HF undergoing RAASi therapy, as well as the efficacy and safety of NPBs in optimizing RAASi therapy.

Combination therapy can enhance treatment efficacy and improve patient outcomes through the synergistic effects of different medications. Treatment guidelines recommend combination therapy as the standard treatment strategy for patients with HF or CKD. Our findings reveal an overall pooled HK incidence of 10.0% among RAASi users, with higher rates in CKD patients (12.0%) compared to HF patients (9.2%). Additionally, in the incidence statistics of HK, the rate in the group with K ≥ 5.5 mmol/L was higher than that in the group with K ≥ 5.0 mmol/L. This may be attributed to the relatively smaller number of studies included for the K ≥ 5.0 mmol/L group, which may result in less comprehensive or more variable statistical outcomes for this group. Notably, the risk of HK was significantly associated with factors such as low baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), diabetes, and MRA usage. Subgroup analysis indicated that the use of MRA in combination with ACEI/ARB/ARNI appeared to increase the risk of HK, which may be due to the synergistic effects of RAAS inhibition and aldosterone blockade, both of which promote potassium retention in the kidneys. The result was also confirmed by Sun et al, showing that the co-administration of MRA and ACEi/ARB had beneficial effects on renal outcomes but was associated with an increased incidence of HK []. However, the addition of SGLT2i to these regimens appeared to reduce the risk of HK. Adding SGLT2i to combination therapies containing MRA and ACEI/ARB/ARNI reduced the risk of HK to as low as 1.6% for ACEI/ARB/ARNi + SGLT2i and 4.8% for ACEi/ARB/ARNi + SGLT2i + MRA. This suggests that SGLT2i may play a protective role in regulating blood potassium levels by reducing the risk of HK, potentially through mechanisms such as increasing the negative charge in renal tubules and modulating aldosterone [].

Traditional potassium-lowering therapies, such as sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS) and calcium polystyrene sulfonate (CPS), have been used as treatments for HK in clinical practice for over 60 years. However, due to their varying onset of action, they are not able to achieve rapid potassium elimination and are often associated with significant gastrointestinal adverse effects. The development of novel SZC and patiromer, has revolutionized the management of HK.

Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate is an insoluble, non-absorbable, non-polymer inorganic material that selectively exchanges sodium and hydrogen ions for potassium ions in the gastrointestinal tract, thereby reducing serum potassium levels through fecal excretion. Patiromer is an organic, sodium-free, non-absorbed polymer designed to exchange potassium for calcium throughout the gastrointestinal tract but mostly in the colon. In multiple clinical trials, both drugs have demonstrated a rapid and sustained reduction in serum potassium levels, along with good safety and tolerability profile [, , , ]. Our meta-analysis demonstrated that NPBs effectively reduced serum potassium levels (by 0.71 mEq/L) and HK events (by 28%) compared to placebo. Furthermore, NPBs increased the proportion of patients achieving RAASi optimization by 38%, with greater efficacy observed in CKD patients than HF patients (84% vs 29%). These findings align with prior meta-analyses, which showed substantial potassium-lowering effects and facilitated higher RAASi dosing in CKD and HF populations.

Subgroup analysis revealed distinct differences in treatment responses between CKD and HF populations, with CKD patients demonstrating a higher optimization rate of RAASi therapy, while HF patients had a greater risk of hypokalemia events (RR = 8.65; 95% CI 2.05–36.53). This phenomenon may be attributed to the distinct pathophysiological characteristics of HF and CKD patients. In HF patients, diuretics are commonly used to reduce cardiac load, but their use may lead to increased potassium excretion. Therefore, when NPBs (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors) are administered, HF patients are more prone to developing hypokalemia. In contrast, CKD patients have impaired renal function, which may make their tolerance to RAASi different from that of HF patients. Additionally, the current number of studies included and sample sizes are still limited, necessitating further confirmation through large randomized controlled trials [, ]. Safety analysis indicated that NPB use was associated with increased risk of hypokalemia (RR 4.96; 95% CI 1.65–14.88), edema (RR 3.10; 95% CI 1.05–9.22), and constipation (RR 2.26; 95% CI 1.01–5.05), emphasizing the need for careful patient selection and monitoring during treatment.

For clinicians managing CKD and HF patients, the use of NPBs should be considered as part of an integrated approach to treatment. Regular monitoring of potassium levels is essential, especially in patients on RAASi therapy. The serum potassium levels and other relevant biochemical indicators should be closely monitored to ensure treatment safety and efficacy. For patients at risk of hypokalemia or HK, or those who have previously experienced either condition, it is recommended to increase potassium monitoring frequency to at least once a month [, ]. When elevated potassium levels are detected, the addition of an NPB should be considered, even if the potassium increase is not yet at clinically significant levels. Novel potassium binders can be dosed flexibly based on individual patient needs, and their introduction should be guided by the severity of HK and the patient’s renal function. In addition, combining RAASi with SGLT2i should be prioritized, as this combination reduces the risk of HK compared to regimens without SGLT2i. Education for patients on the importance of medication adherence and monitoring is also crucial to ensure the optimal outcomes from these therapies.

Although this meta-analysis provides robust evidence, it is limited by the heterogeneity in study populations and varying definitions of HK thresholds. Additionally, the long-term effects of potassium binders on clinical endpoints, such as mortality and disease progression, remain underexplored due to the limited follow-up duration of most included studies. Despite these limitations, this study’s strength lies in its synthesis of data from diverse populations, enhancing the generalizability of our findings.

In conclusion, HK poses a frequent and significant barrier to the optimal use of RAASi therapy in patients with CKD and HF. The NPBs effectively reduce HK incidence and allow RAASi optimization. However, their use necessitates careful consideration of potential AEs, particularly hypokalemia and edema. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating NPBs as an integral component of comprehensive HK management strategies, with the ultimate goal of improving outcomes for patients with CKD and HF.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitor treatment is associated with high prevalence of HK, especially in bigeminal and triple therapy. Potassium binders are effective in RAASi optimization and HK management, especially among the CKD population.
